_README: Single source of the book's structure; the build is driven entirely by this file. This is NOT a translation: the source (Harold Isaacs, The Tragedy of the Chinese Revolution, Haymarket Books 2009, a reprint of the Secker & Warburg 1938 first edition) is already in English, with a clean born-digital text layer. The job is an ANNOTATED ENGLISH EDITION: Isaacs's own text preserved verbatim in out/<id>_reading.md, his own numbered endnotes converted to popup footnotes, PLUS a new reader-facing footnote layer, a glossary of names/terms, and a Principal Characters page. 'edition_kind' below switches the builder's chrome from translation wording to edition wording. Cite the book's PRINTED FOLIO in notes (arabic in the body, roman in the front matter), never the PDF page.

description: Harold Isaacs's classic history of the second Chinese revolution of 1925-1927 and its defeat. Written by a young American journalist who had lived and worked in China, and first published in London in 1938 with an introduction by Leon Trotsky, it is a documented, polemical account of the alliance between the Communists and the Kuomintang, its bloody collapse at Shanghai and Wuhan, and the role of the Communist International under Stalin. This annotated edition preserves Isaacs's 1938 text and its own reference notes, and adds a reader-facing layer of explanatory footnotes, a glossary of names and terms in the Wade-Giles romanization Isaacs used (with pinyin), and a guide to the principal figures, for readers with no background in modern Chinese history.

translator_note: This is an annotated reading edition of The Tragedy of the Chinese Revolution by Harold R. Isaacs, reset from the Haymarket Books (2009) reprint of the first edition (Secker & Warburg, London, 1938). Isaacs's text is reproduced as printed; nothing in the narrative has been rewritten, modernized, or abridged.

Two kinds of note appear at the foot of the page. Isaacs's own reference notes — the numbered citations he gathered at the back of the book — have been moved to the point in the text they document, so a reader can see the source without turning to the endmatter. To these has been added a second, editorial layer: brief notes identifying the people, places, institutions, offices, and party and Comintern terms that a reader without a background in modern Chinese history would not be expected to know, and flagging, where it is checkable, whether a claim is corroborated by later scholarship. Editorial notes are marked as such; every other note is Isaacs's own.

Isaacs wrote in the Wade-Giles romanization standard in the 1930s (Chiang Kai-shek, Borodin, Kuomintang, Wuhan). His spellings are kept in the text. The glossary and the notes give the modern pinyin form and, where useful, the Chinese characters, so that a name here can be matched to one in a present-day account.

The book is a partisan work, written from a Trotskyist standpoint and carrying an introduction by Trotsky himself. The editorial notes try to mark where the account is shaped by that standpoint, and where its factual claims have held up, without arguing with the author.
source_note: Born-digital PDF (Haymarket 2009), 409 pages, clean embedded text layer (QuarkXPress/Quartz), no OCR needed. Bookmarks present and accurate. Front matter runs a roman-numeral sequence (i-xxii); the body restarts at arabic 1. Body offset is constant: printed = (PDF page, 1-indexed) - 23, verified at every chapter opener. In-text reference marks are 5.5pt superscript digits, numbered per chapter; the endnotes run printed 340-373, the index 374 to the end.
